text: Classical Athens filled its Council of 500, its jury panels and most public offices by lot. Aristotle recorded the common view that selection by lot was democratic and election oligarchic.
According to Plutarch, an illiterate voter asked Aristides the Just to scratch 'Aristides' on his ostracism shard, being tired of hearing him called the Just. Aristides wrote his own name.
Political 'left' and 'right' come from the French National Assembly of 1789, where supporters of a royal veto sat to the president's right and its opponents to his left.
Duverger's law: elections in single-member districts won by a plurality, as in Britain and the US, tend to produce two dominant parties, because voters desert third parties they expect to lose.
Condorcet showed in 1785 that majorities can go in circles: a group can prefer A to B and B to C by majority vote, yet also prefer C to A, so 'the will of the majority' may not exist.
Political scientist Jack Levy called the absence of war between democracies the closest thing to an empirical law in international relations. Why it holds is still debated.

The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is often said to have founded the system of sovereign states, yet its treaties say nothing about sovereignty as a principle; scholar Andreas Osiander calls this the Westphalian myth.
In the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, Spain and Portugal split the non-European world along a meridian 370 leagues west of Cape Verde. The line put Brazil's eastern bulge on Portugal's side.

The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 did not actually carve up Africa on a map. It set rules for claiming territory, and most African borders were fixed later through bilateral deals among colonial powers.
"The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." (Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, c. 400 BCE)
About a fifth of the world's oil consumption, roughly 20 million barrels a day in 2024, passed through the Strait of Hormuz, which at its narrowest is only about 39 km (24 miles) wide.

On 26 September 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov saw his early-warning system report US missile launches and judged it a false alarm instead of passing it up the chain. Sunlight on clouds had fooled the satellites.
Studying 323 campaigns from 1900 to 2006, Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan found that major nonviolent resistance movements succeeded about 53% of the time, against 26% for violent ones.
After the only slave revolt to found a nation, Haiti was made to pay France 150 million francs in 1825, under threat of warships, to compensate former slaveholders; related debts ran until 1947.
Magna Carta failed within weeks: sealed in June 1215, it was annulled by Pope Innocent III that August. Reissued versions survived, and three of its clauses are still law in England and Wales.
Switzerland has no single leader. A seven-member Federal Council acts collectively as head of state and government, and its president, elected for one year, is first among equals.
In 1983 Benedict Anderson called nations 'imagined communities': members will never meet or even hear of most of their compatriots, yet each carries in mind an image of their communion.
When Italy unified in 1861, only about 2.5% of its people could speak standard Italian properly, by linguist Tullio De Mauro's estimate; most spoke regional languages and dialects.
Amartya Sen argued that no substantial famine has ever occurred in an independent democracy with a relatively free press, because elections and newspapers make famine politically fatal for rulers.
San Marino, which by tradition dates its founding to 301, has two heads of state at once: the Captains Regent, elected for six-month terms in a system that goes back at least to 1243.
"This body which called itself and which still calls itself the Holy Roman Empire was in no way holy, nor Roman, nor an empire." (Voltaire, Essai sur les moeurs, 1756)
At its peak the East India Company, a London trading firm owned by shareholders, commanded private armies of about 260,000 soldiers, at times twice the size of the British Army.
Spain's national anthem, the Marcha Real, has never had official lyrics, so it is played without words. The anthems of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo are also wordless.

In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth a single deputy could dissolve the Sejm and void its laws by declaring 'Nie pozwalam' ('I do not allow'). This liberum veto lasted until the Constitution of 3 May 1791.
"And the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651)
Russia's Big Diomede and America's Little Diomede lie about 3.8 km apart in the Bering Strait, but the International Date Line runs between them, so their clocks differ by 21 hours (20 in summer).
The United Nations began in 1945 with 51 member states. Decolonization and the breakup of federations nearly quadrupled that; South Sudan became the 193rd member in 2011.

Britain's 1739 War of Jenkins' Ear with Spain is named for a sea captain whose ear a Spanish coast guard cut off in 1731. The tale that he showed the preserved ear to Parliament has no corroborating record.
Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, soon after being imprisoned and tortured by the restored Medici, partly hoping to win their favor. It was published only in 1532, five years after his death.
Australia has made voting compulsory in federal elections since 1924, with small fines for not turning up. Turnout has stayed around or above 90 percent, far higher than in most democracies.
